thread.title: Cypress Semiconductor's Value Obscured By A Growing Wall Of Worry - Cypress Semiconductor Corporation (NASDAQ:CY)

author: Stephen Simpson, CFA
title: Cypress Semiconductor's Value Obscured By A Growing Wall Of Worry - Cypress Semiconductor Corporation (NASDAQ:CY)
text:
Given the roughly 15% drop in the SOX over the past six months, it’s not too hard to find chip stocks that look more reasonably-valued, if not cheap, these days. The catch, though, is how well current expectations factor in the numerous risks that seem to be mounting early in 2019 – shrinking lead-times, weakening auto and industrial markets, weakening memory pricing, and so on. Although I do like the business mix at Cypress ( CY ), and I believe the company is well-placed to gain share in the auto and IoT markets in the years to come, weaker near-term conditions are definitely a risk and I think it will take some time before a margin-driven mid-to-high teens fair value gains any real traction in the market.
Lead-Times And Pricing Are Weakening As I’ve written in relation to ON Semiconductor ( ON ) and other chip companies, record lead-times from back in the summer are now at last correcting. Although it was inevitable that this would happen, the correction has picked up some steam lately, creating more risks for revenue/orders in the next few quarters. Although past experience is no guarantee of the future, the semiconductor industry rarely sees graceful dismounts from peak lead-times, so I wouldn’t underestimate the potential turbulence as distributors and customers get their inventories back in line.
As highlighted in a recent report from Susquehana analyst Christopher Rolland, lead-times for Cypress have fallen about two weeks from their peak, one of the more significant drops among peers like STMicrolectronics ( STM ) (which has seen a 6-week drop), NXP Semiconductors ( NXPI ) (half a week), and ON (about a week and a half). For Cypress, it has been a double-barreled correction, with both NOR flash and microcontrollers (or MCUs) seeing significant lead-time declines. Not surprisingly, with lead-times falling, pricing has started to slip, with NOR prices down almost double-digits early in December.
Making matters worse, the macro situation is shaky and unpredictable. The U.S. auto market has held up pretty well, with a good December (up 1.6%) boosting the full-year number to 0.6% growth, but China and Europe have weakened more significantly, and it looks like the weakness in Europe is extending beyond emissions testing-related disruptions. With Cypress generating about a third of its revenue from the auto market, that’s no minor concern, even if content gains can still help revenue (Cypress still has new business wins rolling in, including the Toyota ( TM ) Corolla).
And it’s not just the auto market. The industrial sector is looking softer, with China leading the way on considerable tariff-related uncertainty. Not only did Cypress have one of the more serious negative revisions for the fourth quarter, but management cited the tariff issue with segments like APAC consumer IoT.
How memory fares for Cypress in 2019 will be interesting to see. Bulls go to some lengths to highlight the fact that Cypress has concentrated on higher-value (and higher-density) markets like autos (about 50% of revenue) and that 70% of the business is under long-term contracts. I still wouldn’t overlook the risks, though, of portions of that 70% underperforming on weaker volumes, while the remaining uncontracted 30% sees steeper pricing pressures.
Strong Assets In Attractive Markets Although the next two to six quarters could be rocky for Cypress and the sector at large, I like how this company is built for the future. Between a strong position in automotive and IoT MCUs and connectivity, complemented by a very profitable memory business, I think Cypress is well-placed to leverage increasing auto chip content and what should be significant growth in consumer and industrial IoT. A lack of exciting data center exposure is a modest negative, but I’d also note that Cypress has very little downside risk to slowing handset volumes.
While Cypress is not a large player in MCUs, with mid-single-digit share that is well behind the likes of Renesas ( OTCPK:RNECY ), Microchip ( MCHP ), and STM, they are still in the top 10 and I would argue they punch above their weight by virtue of a focused market strategy. The company is third or fourth-largest auto MCU supplier now (behind Renesas and NXP) and holds close to 40% share in the MCUs used in instrumentation clusters. Chip content growth in autos is a well-understood trend, but I would note that Cypress continues to position itself for growth markets like ADAS (working with practically every player) and “body electronics”.
Market share data are less reliable in IoT, but what data I can find lend credence to the notion that Cypress is a leader in consumer IoT (with big-name wins like Amazon ’s ( AMZN ) Echo) and the Nintendo ( OTCPK:NTDOY ) Switch) and staking out a solid position in some industrial IoT markets.
Complementing the MCU business is a strong connectivity business that got a major boost when Broadcom ( AVGO ) decided to get out of the business and sell its connectivity assets to Cypress. That transaction made Cypress a force in WiFi and Bluetooth, the two most popular connectivity technologies. While Silicon Labs ( SLAB ) boasts a broader array of wireless technologies, including Z-wave and a strong presence in Zigbee (where Cypress is also present), some of these technologies require a more missionary sale process than WiFi and Bluetooth, and I believe Cypress has a stronger technology position in MCUs, which is a competitive advantage given the increasing focus on integrated solutions (combining an MCU and wireless capability).
To be clear, I think there’s room for both Cypress and Silicon Labs to succeed, and I think the strength of their connectivity assets could make either (or both) acquisition targets for companies with stronger MCU portfolios and/or a desire to move into these markets. Turning back to Cypress, the company has over 60% share in auto connectivity (WiFi and Bluetooth) and I expect meaningful growth in IoT device volumes in the years to come.
And The Rest… Largely for the interest of brevity, I’ll keep my discussion of Cypress’s USB-C and memory businesses short. Cypress has an early strong lead in UBS-C (with roughly 35% share) and has won Apple ’s ( AAPL ) business, but UBS-C is a small market at present. While I believe there are meaningful growth opportunities that will expand the market (Cypress has been working with Panasonic on replacing TV HDMI with UBS-C), I think competition from companies like ON and NXP and new entrants will mitigate those benefits.
In memory, Cypress has a strong presence in NOR memory and SRAM (where it is the leader). Cypress has parlayed its NOR business into roughly 65% share of the auto NOR flash market, and growth in applications like advanced ADAS should expand the market further, but memory is on the whole a legacy business for Cypress and one that isn’t a priority for R&D or capex dollars. To that end, the company recently sold its NAND flash business into a JV with SK Hynix and although the legacy business is quite profitable, I don’t expect it to be a growth driver and those rich margins could be vulnerable if there are protracted price declines in NOR memory.
The Outlook I like how Cypress has become more gross margin-focused under CEO Hassane El-Khoury, including selling the NAND business into the JV, managing the remaining memory business as a cash cow operation, and using external fabs for sub-55nm processes. I also like the willingness to walk away from business with inadequate margins – something that has served companies like Broadcom and Linear well in their businesses.
I don’t have a lot of confidence in the near-term outlook for the chip sector, as it is difficult to model orders and revenue during lead-time corrections. To that end, I’d note that Cypress’s 0.8 book-to-bill in the third quarter was the lowest figure in five years. I do believe content and unit growth in the auto sector and strong growth in IoT can support a mid-single-digit long-term revenue growth rate, but there could be above-average turbulence (misses and revisions) over the next few quarters as the market finds the new normal and end-markets like auto sort themselves out.
I do see room for more gross margin and operating margin improvement, and this is an area where Cypress still underperforms (they’re well shy of the 60/30 targets for semiconductor GM/OPM). I believe adjusted FCF margins could improve by around four points over the next decade, supporting high single-digit FCF growth.
Translating that all into valuation, I believe Cypress is slightly undervalued on a discounted cash flow basis. Near-term margins and revenue growth tend to have a stronger influence on chip stock valuations, though, and I believe an EV/revenue multiple of 3x is fair today, supporting a fair value of $16.50. A similar approach that works through EV/EBITDA drives a lower fair value of $13.
The Bottom Line All told, I think $13 to $17 is a reasonable range for Cypress’s fair value today, and given that the shares trade below $13, I think this is a name worth a closer look. I do think there is above-average risk over the next few quarters (more due to macro factors than company-specific execution), but Cypress’s position in auto and IoT MCUs, connectivity, and memory makes it a name to at least consider for a watch list.
Disclosure: I am/we are long AVGO. I wrote this article myself, and it expresses my own opinions. I am not receiving compensation for it (other than from Seeking Alpha). I have no business relationship with any company whose stock is mentioned in this article.
